content: Higher consumption of omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFA), such as those found in fish, during pregnancy has been linked to longer gestational periods and improved perinatal outcomes. This review aimed to evaluate the effects of omega-3 LCPUFA supplementation or dietary intake during pregnancy on maternal, perinatal, neonatal, and longer-term outcomes for both mother and child. For this updated review, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included if they compared omega-3 LCPUFA (as supplements or dietary sources) with placebo or no omega-3, or if they directly compared different doses or types of omega-3 LCPUFA. A total of 70 RCTs involving 19,927 pregnant women were analyzed. The trials included women at varying levels of risk for adverse pregnancy outcomes, with most studies conducted in upper-middle or high-income countries. The findings showed that omega-3 LCPUFA supplementation reduced the risk of preterm birth (<37 weeks) from 13.4% to 11.9% (risk ratio [RR] 0.89, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.81 to 0.97) and early preterm birth (<34 weeks) from 4.6% to 2.7% (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.77). Both outcomes were supported by high-quality evidence. However, there was a slight increase in the likelihood of prolonged gestation (>42 weeks) from 1.6% to 2.6% (RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.11 to 2.33), based on moderate-quality evidence. For infants, there was a possible reduction in the risk of perinatal death (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.03) and neonatal care admissions (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.03), though these findings were based on moderate-quality evidence. The risk of low birthweight (LBW) was reduced from 15.6% to 14% (RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.82 to 0.99), supported by high-quality evidence. However, there was a potential small increase in the risk of large-for-gestational-age (LGA) infants (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.36), based on moderate-quality evidence. No significant differences were observed in the rates of small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infants or intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR). For maternal outcomes, there was insufficient evidence to determine the effects of omega-3 LCPUFA on post-term labor induction, maternal serious adverse events, maternal intensive care unit (ICU) admissions, or postnatal depression. However, the mean gestational length was slightly longer in women who received omega-3 LCPUFA (mean difference [MD] 1.67 days, 95% CI 0.95 to 2.39). There was also a possible reduction in the risk of pre-eclampsia (RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.01), though this was based on low-quality evidence. For child and adult outcomes, there were minimal differences between omega-3 LCPUFA supplementation and no omega-3 in terms of cognition, IQ, vision, neurodevelopment, growth, language, and behavior. Most of these findings were based on lowto very low-quality evidence. The effect of omega-3 LCPUFA on body mass index (BMI) at 19 years of age was uncertain (MD 0, 95% CI -0.83 to 0.83), and no data were available on the development of diabetes in the children of study participants. In conclusion, omega-3 LCPUFA supplementation during pregnancy effectively reduces the risk of preterm birth and early preterm birth, though it may slightly increase the incidence of post-term pregnancies. The evidence for other maternal, neonatal, and long-term outcomes is less robust, with many findings limited by study design and imprecision. Further follow-up of completed trials is needed to better understand the long-term effects on metabolic, growth, and neurodevelopmental pathways, as well as to explore the impact of different types, doses, and timing of omega-3 LCPUFA supplementation.
